paras: The attempted lynching of Liberty Kennedy took place in Hannibal, Missouri, on August 22, 1882, when a crowd of white citizens chased down Kennedy, a young Black man accused with Edward Murphy of assaulting a white girl, and relatives of the girl tried to kill him. The attempt failed and both men were jailed, but the wire dispatch that carried the story across the country predicted they would be lynched at their examination.

According to a Hannibal special to the St. Louis Republican, Kennedy and Murphy attacked Dora Kimball, a white girl reported as six years old, as she walked along the railroad track in the western suburbs of the city about noon. The dispatch said the two men dragged her into the woods or "high weeds" by the roadside, where D. H. Courtney, driving past in a wagon, came upon them.

Courtney seized Murphy and took him to police headquarters. A "great crowd of excited citizens" then turned out after Kennedy, in one version "to hunt" him and in another "to hang" him. After a long chase he was captured, but before he reached jail relatives of the girl who were in the pursuing party made what the dispatch called "an ineffectual attempt at killing him." A shorter version of the dispatch named the girl's father as the man who made the attempt.

Both prisoners were held for an examination, at which, the dispatches said, "it is thought they will be lynched." Later summaries reported only that both men were in jail and that "Lynching is talked of." No report of the examination, a lynching, an indictment or a trial was found in the coverage.

The story reached the white press through the wire and ran from August 23 to early September in papers in St. Paul, Omaha, Memphis, Sacramento, Helena, Bismarck, Elko, Raleigh, Roseburg and Benton. Every paper printed the accusation as fact, describing the girl as "outraged" and the men as "ravishers" or "negroes," and none questioned the expected lynching. Headlines varied in emphasis: the Omaha Daily Bee announced "A Lynching Party Promised," the Sacramento Daily Record-Union "Two Lives in Jeopardy," and the Bismarck Tribune "Black Ravishers in Peril," while the Benton Weekly Record called the men "Two Colored Brutes."
Small differences crept in as the dispatch was condensed: Kennedy appeared as "Jno." and "L. I." Kennedy, and the Memphis Daily Appeal gave the girl's age as sixteen.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Liberty Kennedy
bases: A crowd of white citizens pursued Kennedy, reportedly 'to hang' him, and the girl's relatives in the pursuing party tried to kill him before he was jailed; papers expected both prisoners to be lynched (A1, A2, A5).
No one was killed: the relatives' attempt on Kennedy was 'ineffectual' and both men were lodged in jail (A1, A2); no later report of a lynching was found, so this is an attempted lynching only.
Every account is a version of one Hannibal special to the St. Louis Republican carried by the wire (A7), reprinted with small variations (A1, A2, A5); no independent or local account was found.

accounts.gist: Same story, but names Kennedy 'Jno.' and says the girl's father made the attempt on his life.

framing.detail: Papers from St. Paul to Sacramento ran the dispatch as fact under headlines like 'Ravishers Captured' and 'A Brutal Outrage', calling the girl 'outraged' and anticipating a lynching without comment.
Headlines centered the threat to the prisoners, 'A Lynching Party Promised', 'Two Lives in Jeopardy', 'Black Ravishers in Peril', while the Benton Weekly Record called them 'Two Colored Brutes'.
